extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in research integrity, academic researchers, and science journalists
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and reporting on allegations of scientific misconduct, subsequent investigations, retractions, and institutional responses in academic research. Focuses on criteria for judging the reliability of findings, adequacy of investigations, and appropriate corrective actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Findings of scientific misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal investigation found him guilty of eight counts of scientific misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A formal investigative finding of misconduct (numbered counts, documented investigation) is a primary criterion for judging a case; such findings justify corrective actions (e.g., retraction, sanctions). Where present, they should be reported and treated as authoritative unless overturned on appeal. Example: the university committee's conclusion described in the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction following investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Retracted a paper last year following a university investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retraction of publications is an appropriate corrective measure when an investigation shows data or conduct problems that undermine the paper. Use retraction status to assess the reliability of the published record; investigators and readers should treat retracted findings with caution and note retraction notices when evaluating prior work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent replication as validation
rubrics_metrics.description: Hauser ‘replicated’ his own study. Most would not consider it a replication until someone else replicates the result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replication by independent researchers is the gold standard for validating contested results. Self-replication is an insufficient validation due to potential bias. When evaluating a disputed finding, prioritize independent replications; explicitly note when claimed replications are performed by the original author as an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest undermines validation
rubrics_metrics.description: He has a major conflict of interest, to say the least.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflicts of interest (especially when the original author attempts to reproduce their own work) reduce confidence in reproduced results. Best practice: require disclosure of conflicts and favor independent verification; treat undisclosed or significant conflicts as a factor reducing evidentiary weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional precautionary measures (teaching/restrictions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A large majority of the Harvard psychology faculty had voted not to allow him to teach this year, and Faculty of Arts and Sciences Dean Michael D. Smith had supported the decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions may restrict duties (teaching, supervision) as a precaution pending/after investigations. Such measures are relevant criteria when assessing institutional response adequacy and protecting students/trainees. Document faculty votes, administrative statements, and the scope/duration of restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Career consequences and resignation
rubrics_metrics.description: Marc Hauser has resigned his position as a faculty member, effective August 1, 2011.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resignation, termination, or departure from posts are concrete outcomes of misconduct cases and signal serious consequences. When assessing the case, record such outcomes and consider them alongside formal findings and retractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact on collaborators
rubrics_metrics.description: I hope his collaborators who acted in good faith aren't too tarnished by the scandal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate and explicitly consider the effect of a misconduct case on coauthors and collaborators. Distinguish between those implicated in misconduct and those who acted in good faith; avoid unfairly attributing blame without evidence. Guidance: review collaborators' roles and available documentation before assigning culpability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for stronger planning and oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Scandal like this can set back genuine research, as people are more reluctant to become involved. need more in depth investigation at the planning stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Robust planning, preregistration, oversight, and in-depth methodological review at study design stage can reduce risks of misconduct or questionable practices. As a criterion for good research, prioritize clear protocols, oversight mechanisms, and pre-study review to prevent later disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical scrutiny and suspicion of data selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistical analysis of his results concluded that they were impossibly good. Apparently, he cherry-picked his results because he knew nothing about statistics…
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improbably good or 'too perfect' statistical results should trigger closer scrutiny for possible selective reporting or data manipulation. Evaluate raw data, analysis choices, and reporting transparency. Look for signs of cherry-picking, p-hacking, or undisclosed exclusions as red flags.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and investigative reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Boston Globe’s Carolyn Johnson, who broke the original Hauser retraction story, reports... David Dobbs has also been doing good analysis of the case at Neuron Culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independent journalism and transparent reporting are important for uncovering and explaining misconduct cases. Use credible media investigations and expert analysis as sources of contextual information, while corroborating their claims against primary documents (investigation reports, retraction notices). Cite such reporting when summarizing a case, but distinguish between reporting and formal institutional findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism about self-reported replication
rubrics_metrics.description: He 'replicated' his own study.  Most would not consider it a replication until someone else replicates the result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat self-reported replication with skepticism; explicitly note the difference between author-led repeat experiments and independent replications. Require independent confirmation before restoring full confidence in disputed results.
